title: Charge-selective topological locking and ultraslow coarsening in magnetoelastic media
abstract: We demonstrate that the symmetry of magnetoelastic coupling governs the topological organization of composite defects and can qualitatively alter phase-ordering kinetics. In a two-dimensional theory of an in-plane magnetic vector coupled to elastic strain, we find that integer magnetic vortices bind pairs of elementary elastic half-defects. Isotropic magnetostriction produces a core-induced elastic winding independent of the magnetic charge, giving defect binding without charge locking and leaving the magnetic sector with essentially XY-like coarsening. In contrast, quadrupolar magnetoelastic coupling locks magnetic and elastic defect charges: continuous rotational symmetry favors $q_φ=q_θ$, whereas crystalline anisotropy can reverse the locking to $q_φ=-q_θ$. We reveal that both locking sectors display anomalously slow vortex annihilation: defect density shows a power-law decay $t^{-2/5}$, while the average defect-velocity scales as $t^{-4/5}$. These results are consistent with a dynamic exponent $z\simeq 5$. We show that this coarsening slowdown is associated with large anisotropic elastic friction. An adiabatic elimination of the elastic field reveals that isotropic magnetostriction merely renormalizes local magnetic interactions, whereas orientational coupling induces effective nonlocal interactions between magnetic spins. Our experimentally testable results thus establish magnetoelastic coupling symmetry as a means of controlling defect topology and ordering kinetics.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how the symmetry of magnetoelastic coupling governs the topological structure of defects in coupled magnetic and elastic materials. The authors show that quadrupolar coupling enforces specific charge-locking rules, which in turn lead to ultraslow, power-law coarsening kinetics. This establishes symmetry control as a mechanism to tune defect topology and ordering dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the symmetry of magnetoelastic coupling dictates the topological organization of defects and alters the kinetics of phase ordering in coupled magnetic and elastic media.
main_result: Quadrupolar coupling leads to charge-selective topological locking between magnetic and elastic defects, resulting in anomalously slow coarsening dynamics characterized by a power-law decay $t^{-2/5}$ and a dynamic exponent $z \simeq 5$.
method: The analysis involves deriving an effective magnetic free energy by adiabatically eliminating the elastic field and studying the resulting defect dynamics using continuum field theories.
model_or_system: The system is a 2D magnetoelastic medium modeled by a free energy functional coupling an in-plane magnetic order parameter $N(\mathbf{r}, t)$ to an elastic strain field $u(\mathbf{r}, t)$. The coupling includes isotropic and quadrupolar terms.
key_observables: Defect density decay ($\sim t^{-2/5}$), average defect velocity ($\sim t^{-4/5}$), and the topological relationship between elastic ($q_\phi$) and magnetic ($q_	heta$) defect charges.
important_parameters: Coupling coefficients ($c_{	ext{or}}, c_{	ext{sh}}$), which determine the locking regime (e.g., $q_\phi = q_	heta$ vs. $q_\phi = -q_	heta$).
main_assumptions: The dynamics are assumed to be purely relaxational, and the analysis often involves adiabatic elimination of the elastic field.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate defect binding patterns under isotropic vs. quadrupolar coupling, and show the spatial response of coupled fields, highlighting the extended elastic contribution from quadrupolar coupling.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general magnetoelastic free energy, then analyzing the specific topological locking rules dictated by the symmetry of the coupling (isotropic vs. quadrupolar), and finally deriving the effective magnetic Hamiltonian and the resulting slow coarsening kinetics.
why_interesting: The concept of symmetry controlling topological defects and slowing down relaxation dynamics is highly relevant to understanding glassy dynamics, domain coarsening in magnetic materials, and defect physics in condensed matter systems.
